cases.title: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
cases.stem: Ms. Leah Pinto, a 22-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder, comes to the emergency psychiatric service after cutting her forearm superficially following an argument with her partner. She is tearful, angry, and says, “If he leaves me, I’ll kill myself.” She alternates between pleading for reassurance and accusing staff of not caring. She becomes increasingly upset when told she may need observation and says she will hurt herself again if left alone. The nurse must respond without reinforcing maladaptive behaviour while still prioritising safety. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate high immediate risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Escalating anger toward staff
Verbal threat to kill herself
Emotional lability and intense fear of abandonment
Threat to self-harm again if left alone
Recent self-harm behaviour

questions.rationale: All of these findings matter. Borderline personality disorder does not reduce the seriousness of suicidal threats or self-harm. The nurse must take all suicidal content seriously while maintaining consistent boundaries. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient mainly wants attention and should be ignored
The patient is manipulative, so the threats are not serious
The patient has no need for assessment because the injuries are superficial
The patient is emotionally dysregulated with real self-harm risk and requires structured, consistent, safety-focused care

questions.rationale: The patient may show manipulative relational patterns, but the nurse must never dismiss self-harm risk. Structured, nonjudgmental care with clear limits is appropriate. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Social withdrawal
Risk for self-directed violence related to emotional dysregulation and abandonment fears
Disturbed body image
Knowledge deficit about diet

questions.rationale: The priority is immediate safety. Emotional dysregulation and impulsive self-harm are high-risk features. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Address immediate safety, assess suicidal intent and means, set clear boundaries, and maintain a calm consistent approach
Refuse to speak with her because she is manipulative
Promise the patient special treatment if she stops crying
Debate whether she is truly suicidal

questions.rationale: The nurse should assess risk seriously and provide structured, consistent care. Promising special treatment or withdrawing communication may reinforce maladaptive behaviour or worsen escalation. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which responses are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I can see you are very upset. We will deal with one issue at a time.”
“I want to help keep you safe, and we will talk about what happened.”
“You are just trying to manipulate us.”
“We cannot allow self-harm, and we will stay focused on your safety.”
“If you cut again, no one will care.”

questions.rationale: These responses are validating without overinvolvement and set limits without shaming. Judgmental or rejecting statements are inappropriate and may worsen self-harm risk. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Staff respond inconsistently and the patient becomes more volatile
The patient is left alone despite ongoing threats
The patient remains safe, accepts boundaries more consistently, and begins expressing feelings verbally instead of escalating immediately to self-harm threats
The nurse offers special privileges to stop behaviour

questions.rationale: Improvement is measured by safer coping, consistent limit-setting, and reduced reliance on crisis behaviours.

cases.title: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
cases.stem: Mr. Robert D’Mello, a 48-year-old man, is admitted to the medical unit after stopping heavy alcohol use abruptly when he developed gastritis. On the first day he is anxious, tremulous, sweaty, and nauseated. He says he feels like his heart is racing and cannot sleep. By the next shift he becomes more restless and reports seeing insects on the wall. The nurse notes tremor, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, agitation, and visual hallucinations. The nurse recognises progression toward severe alcohol withdrawal and possible delirium tremens. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate severe alcohol withdrawal? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe agitation and insomnia
Tachycardia and hypertension
Tremor and diaphoresis
Visual hallucinations
Recent abrupt cessation of heavy alcohol use

questions.rationale: These are classic signs of escalating alcohol withdrawal. Hallucinations, autonomic instability, and agitation are particularly concerning for severe withdrawal or delirium tremens. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Stable sobriety with no danger
Mild stress only
Schizophrenia onset only
Severe alcohol withdrawal with risk of delirium tremens, seizures, and cardiovascular instability

questions.rationale: This is a high-risk withdrawal pattern. DTs can be life-threatening and require close monitoring and medication management. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Low self-esteem
Social isolation
Disturbed sleep only
Risk for injury, seizure, and autonomic instability related to severe alcohol withdrawal

questions.rationale: Safety and physiological stability are the priorities in severe withdrawal. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Confront the hallucinations by arguing with the patient
Leave the patient alone in a dark room without checks
Delay assessment until the morning
Initiate close withdrawal monitoring, maintain a safe environment, and prepare prescribed withdrawal management promptly

questions.rationale: The patient requires close observation, medication support, and safety measures. Arguing with hallucinations is not helpful, and isolation without monitoring is unsafe. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor vital signs, tremor, orientation, and hallucinations closely
Reduce environmental stimulation while maintaining safety
Encourage hydration and nutrition as tolerated and ordered
Assume hallucinations are harmless if the patient is cooperative
Watch for seizure activity

questions.rationale: Withdrawal may worsen quickly. Hallucinations are not harmless in this context; they signal increasing severity. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Tremor and agitation lessen, vital signs stabilise, hallucinations decrease, and the patient remains safe
Seizure precautions are removed early
Monitoring stops because the patient looks tired
Hallucinations worsen and the patient becomes more disoriented

questions.rationale: Improvement in withdrawal is reflected in autonomic stabilisation, less agitation, and fewer perceptual disturbances.

cases.title: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression
cases.stem: Mr. Sandeep Roy, a 35-year-old man with known opioid misuse, is brought to the emergency department by friends who say they found him difficult to wake. He is pale, breathing slowly, and barely responsive. On assessment, the nurse notes pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate 7 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 84% on room air, and bluish lips. The nurse recognises a likely opioid overdose. Immediate airway and breathing support are essential while emergency reversal and monitoring are prepared. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with opioid overdose? Select all that apply.

options.text: History of opioid misuse
Pinpoint pupils
Hypoxia and cyanosis
Markedly decreased respiratory rate
Reduced responsiveness

questions.rationale: These are classic features of opioid toxicity. Respiratory depression is the most immediate threat to life. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Panic attack only
Alcohol withdrawal
Likely opioid overdose with life-threatening respiratory depression
The patient is sleeping normally

questions.rationale: The priority is recognising opioid overdose as a respiratory emergency. Reduced responsiveness plus pinpoint pupils and bradypnoea are strongly suggestive. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired ventilation and hypoxia related to opioid overdose
Knowledge deficit about exercise
Social isolation
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are always the priority in overdose. Mental health nursing intersects with acute medical safety here. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Support airway and breathing immediately, call for urgent assistance, and prepare for reversal treatment as ordered
Shake the patient and leave if he opens his eyes briefly
Offer oral fluids
Delay intervention until laboratory confirmation

questions.rationale: Immediate respiratory support and emergency response are essential. Waiting for lab confirmation would be unsafe. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous monitoring of respirations, oxygenation, and level of consciousness
Prepare for recurrent sedation after reversal depending on the opioid involved
Maintain patient safety once responsiveness returns
Use calm, direct communication during recovery
Ignore the patient after reversal because the emergency is over

questions.rationale: Opioid overdose management requires ongoing monitoring because respiratory depression may recur. Post-reversal safety and communication are important. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective emergency management?

options.text: The nurse leaves before reassessment
Monitoring is stopped as soon as he wakes up
The patient becomes more cyanotic and unresponsive
Respirations improve, oxygen saturation rises, and the patient becomes more responsive while remaining monitored

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better breathing, better oxygenation, and ongoing observation.

cases.title: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability
cases.stem: Ms. Chloe Martin, a 19-year-old university student, is admitted from an outpatient clinic because of rapid weight loss, dizziness, and near-fainting. She insists that she is “still too large” despite appearing markedly underweight. She reports strict calorie restriction, excessive exercise, and feeling cold most of the time. On assessment, the nurse notes body mass significantly below expected, dry skin, bradycardia, low blood pressure, and obsessional thoughts about food and body size. Chloe denies the seriousness of her condition and says she does not need hospital treatment. The nurse recognises anorexia nervosa with physical instability. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate clinically significant anorexia nervosa? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bradycardia and hypotension
Marked underweight status
Feeling cold and near-fainting
Distorted body image
Excessive exercise and food restriction

questions.rationale: All listed findings are important. The physical signs show medical instability, while body image distortion and extreme control behaviours support the diagnosis. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Ordinary adolescent insecurity only
Healthy dieting with good self-discipline
Stable nutrition with no risk
Eating disorder with serious medical compromise requiring close monitoring

questions.rationale: The patient has both psychological and physiological danger signs. The nurse must not be reassured by the patient’s denial of illness. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for dysrhythmia, syncope, and further physiological deterioration related to malnutrition
Social withdrawal only
Need for gym access
Disturbed sleep alone

questions.rationale: Medical instability is the immediate priority in severe anorexia, particularly bradycardia, low blood pressure, and risk of collapse. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Begin careful medical and nutritional monitoring, assess immediate physical stability, and support structured treatment with therapeutic communication
Leave all decisions entirely to the patient without monitoring
Argue about calories and force food without assessment
Praise the patient’s self-control

questions.rationale: The nurse must balance medical safety with a calm, nonjudgmental approach. Praise or confrontation can reinforce pathology or escalate resistance. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient appearance is the only issue
Watch for refeeding-related complications once nutrition improves
Use neutral, nonjudgmental language about food and weight
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, hydration, and labs closely
Support structured meals as ordered

questions.rationale: Anorexia treatment includes medical monitoring, refeeding safety, and neutral therapeutic communication. The condition is far more serious than appearance concerns. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Anorexia Nervosa with Medical Instability | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates early progress?

options.text: Monitoring stops because the patient says she is fine
Staff argue with the patient about appearance
Vital signs become more stable, the patient tolerates structured intake, and engagement with treatment improves gradually
The patient becomes weaker and vital signs worsen

questions.rationale: Early improvement may be gradual, but stabilising physiology and increased engagement are important indicators.

cases.title: Serotonin Syndrome
cases.stem: Mr. Aaron Lewis, a 30-year-old patient being treated for depression, presents with agitation, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, and muscle rigidity after recently starting a new antidepressant while also using St. John’s Wort from a health food store. He is restless, flushed, and says he feels “wired and sick.” On assessment, the nurse notes elevated temperature, tachycardia, tremor, hyperreflexia, and increasing confusion. The nurse recognises possible serotonin syndrome and the need for urgent intervention. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Agitation and confusion
Recent serotonergic medication change with supplement use
Tremor and hyperreflexia
Sweating and elevated temperature
Diarrhea

questions.rationale: All listed findings are characteristic of serotonin syndrome. This is a high-yield NCLEX medication safety topic in mental health nursing. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Mild anxiety only
Serotonin syndrome requiring urgent medical attention and medication review
Bipolar mania only
Stable antidepressant adjustment

questions.rationale: The combination of autonomic instability, neuromuscular findings, and serotonergic exposure is concerning for serotonin syndrome. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for severe autonomic and neurological instability related to medication interaction
Social anxiety
Mild embarrassment
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The syndrome can become life-threatening. Immediate physical safety and medication review are priorities. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay action until tomorrow
Tell the patient the symptoms are expected and harmless
Give the next antidepressant dose on time
Hold the suspected serotonergic agents, escalate urgently, and monitor vital signs and neurological status closely

questions.rationale: The nurse must respond urgently, because serotonin syndrome can worsen quickly. Continuing serotonergic medications would be unsafe. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Educate the patient later about avoiding unapproved drug-supplement combinations
Obtain a clear medication and supplement history
Reduce stimulation and maintain safety
Ignore diarrhea because only fever matters
Monitor temperature, heart rate, and rigidity

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. A full medication history is essential because interactions often involve prescription and non-prescription substances. Program Area: Mental Health Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Serotonin Syndrome | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Monitoring stops after one review
Agitation lessens, temperature and heart rate improve, and neuromuscular findings begin to settle
Medication causes are not clarified
Rigidity worsens and confusion increases

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduced autonomic and neurological instability.
